summary: Lists general requirements in support of Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS). It does not present solutions, and additional requirements for specific applications are to be specified in separate documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3689 lists general requirements for supporting Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS) over Internet-based systems. It describes what solutions should address, but does not specify a protocol or require providers to offer the service.

subtitle: General requirements for Internet support of emergency telecommunications services.

tldr.problem: Emergency response may depend on public telecommunications, including Internet-based services. The Internet community needed general requirements that were not limited to telephone calls.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes labels, signaling when used, separation of policy from labels, probabilistic better-than-best-effort treatment, and security requirements for authorized emergency traffic.
tldr.outcome: It presents no solutions or protocol changes. More specific application requirements are left to separate documents, and provider support is not mandated by this RFC.

today: RFC 3689 is an Informational requirements document and has not been updated or obsoleted according to the unit metadata. It describes RFC 3690 as a separate document for IP telephony requirements.

sections.title: Why General ETS Requirements Are Needed
sections.content:
Recovery after disasters may depend on immediate access to available telecommunications, including conventional phones, cellular phones and Internet access. RFC 3689 considers how the Internet can support Emergency Telecommunications Service (ETS).

The document says requirements should not assume that every ETS application uses signaling or is a telephone service. It points to the I-Am-Alive database as an example of an emergency application that can operate without a separate signaling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Emergency communication can use more than telephone calls. The RFC includes applications that exchange data without a separate setup message.

sections.title: Scope and Limits
sections.content:
RFC 3689 defines general system requirements and draws on existing emergency-related systems such as GETS and I-Am-Alive. It does not define solutions, protocol enhancements or requirements for every specific application; those details belong in separate documents.

The RFC does not require organizations to accept or support its requirements. It expects provider obligations to be handled through business arrangements such as service-level agreements, and states that service without such an agreement is best effort.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC states general requirements, not a finished technical solution. It also does not force providers to offer emergency service; provider commitments are expected to come from agreements.

sections.title: Labels, Policy and Network Treatment
sections.content:
If signaling conveys that an emergency exists, signaling mechanisms must carry the relevant labels. Labels may appear at different layers or in packet headers, and labels at different layers need not be identical. The RFC defines a label as an identifier, such as a value or bit pattern.

Policy must remain separate from labels: a label identifies a characteristic, while local policy determines how to achieve it and how labels interact. Better-than-best-effort network functionality should focus on probabilities such as reduced loss, jitter or delay, not guarantees. The RFC does not require such functionality to exist or to be available everywhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A label identifies a traffic type, but it does not dictate how a network handles it. Local rules decide the treatment, and the RFC does not promise that emergency traffic will always receive better service.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Design Issues
sections.content:
Only authorized users should receive emergency services. The RFC says authorization mechanisms should support different levels of restriction. Users should consider end-to-end authentication and integrity rather than relying only on one service provider, and a service may offer confidentiality options.

The document separately raises issues rather than requirements. Labels do not by themselves provide admission control, accounting should not be precluded, and verifying digital signatures can create a denial-of-service risk if an attacker floods a system with invalid labelled data.
sections.plainLanguage: Emergency access needs checks that reject unauthorized use and detect changed messages. Labels alone cannot reserve network capacity, and checking digital signatures can itself be overwhelmed by a flood of invalid messages.
